drills.q: State the three conditions for covariance stationarity and give one financial series that clearly violates each.
drills.a: Constant mean (violated by trending prices), constant variance (violated by volatility clustering in returns), autocovariance depending only on lag not time (violated by a series whose correlation structure shifts across a regime change). Most raw financial levels violate all three simultaneously.

drills.q: Why does one first-difference turn a random walk into white noise? Show the algebra.
drills.a: y_t = y_t-1 + e_t, so dy_t = y_t - y_t-1 = e_t, which by construction has constant mean 0, constant variance, and zero autocovariance at every lag -- the definition of white noise.

drills.q: You compute an ADF t-stat of -2.00 on a series's levels. The 5% critical value is -2.86. What do you conclude, and what test would you run next before finalizing that conclusion?
drills.a: Fail to reject the unit-root null -- the series appears non-stationary in levels. But -2.00 is not far from -2.86, and ADF has low power near phi~1, so run KPSS as a cross-check before committing to d=1.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why an AR(p) process's PACF cuts off after lag p but its ACF does not.
drills.a: PACF at lag k is the direct coefficient of y_t-k in a joint regression on lags 1..k; for k>p, AR(p) has no direct dependence beyond lag p, so that coefficient is exactly zero. ACF is a raw pairwise correlation with no conditioning, so it keeps picking up the dependency propagated indirectly through the AR recursion at every lag, decaying but never cutting off.

drills.q: Given PACF lags 1-2 of 0.479 and -0.444 (both far outside a +/-0.139 band) and every subsequent lag inside the band except a borderline -0.149 at lag 5, what order would you identify and why isn't lag 5 evidence of a longer AR order?
drills.a: AR(2). With 10 lags tested at a 5% significance band, roughly 0.5 false crossings are expected by chance alone; a single borderline crossing five lags past a clean 2-lag cutoff is consistent with sampling noise around a true AR(2), not a real AR(5) structure.

drills.q: A colleague says ACF and PACF are 'the same thing normalized differently.' Correct them with a concrete example.
drills.a: They measure different quantities. For AR(1) with phi=0.8, ACF(2) = phi^2 = 0.64 (the indirect 2-lag chain through lag 1), but PACF(2) = 0 exactly (no direct 2-lag effect once lag 1 is conditioned on). Not the same number rescaled -- different questions answered.

drills.q: Your auto_arima pipeline selects d=2 and produces forecast intervals that explode in width. Diagnose.
drills.a: Likely over-differencing -- the series probably only needed d=0 or d=1. Check ADF/KPSS on the d=1 series before accepting d=2; look for the over-differencing signature (a large isolated negative ACF spike at lag 1 with nothing else significant), and compare AIC/variance between the d=1 and d=2 versions directly.

drills.q: Two unrelated trending revenue series show R^2=0.93 and a highly significant OLS slope when regressed on each other. What's the likely explanation and how do you avoid being fooled by it?
drills.a: Spurious regression (Granger-Newbold 1974) -- two independently non-stationary series produce inflated R^2 and t-stats with disturbing regularity even with zero true relationship. Test both series for stationarity before regressing; if both have unit roots, use cointegration testing (Engle-Granger/Johansen) instead of levels OLS.

drills.q: A monthly revenue ARIMA pipeline re-selects a different (p,d,q) order almost every month via auto_arima, and forecasts swing wildly even though revenue is stable. Diagnose and propose a fix, staff-level.
drills.a: Likely causes: (1) short series relative to search space, so AIC differences between neighboring orders are noisy and flip month to month; (2) no seasonal specification (m=12) forcing the search to crudely approximate annual seasonality with unstable high-order AR/MA terms. Fix: constrain the search with domain knowledge (m=12, modest P/D/Q bounds), widen the training window, and consider refitting less frequently rather than abandoning automated selection.

drills.q: When would you deliberately choose BIC over AIC for ARIMA order selection, and what's the tradeoff?
drills.a: When the goal is a parsimonious, interpretable model of the underlying process (e.g., explaining structure to a risk committee) rather than pure forecast accuracy -- BIC's k*ln(n) penalty is heavier at large n and more likely to recover the true sparse model. Tradeoff: AIC is asymptotically better for one-step-ahead prediction accuracy, so a BIC-selected model can underfit slightly relative to what minimizes forecast error.

drills.q: Why do you need to check whether a seasonal series' seasonal pattern is itself drifting before choosing classical decomposition vs STL?
drills.a: Classical decomposition estimates one fixed seasonal profile applied identically to every cycle across the whole series; if the seasonal shape genuinely evolves (e.g., a holiday peak shifting a week earlier over several years), classical decomposition blurs that real evolving structure into the noise/remainder term. STL's Loess-based approach lets the seasonal component adapt over time and captures it correctly.
